---
title: "Decision Models with tidyllm"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE
)
options(width = 90)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyllm)
library(tidyverse)
```

A chat model writes text. It composes a reply one word at a time, each word chosen given the words before it. A *decision model* works differently: it reads a text and a fixed list of questions, and answers each question without writing any text.

Think of a trained coder filling in a coding form, next to an essay writer. The coder ticks one box per question: yes or no, one category, or a point on a scale. Survey researchers hire coders for exactly this job, and a decision model does the same.

Because the model writes no sentences, it has nothing to compose word by word. That makes it fast and cheap. Vendors list prices of roughly 4 to 10 US cents per million input tokens (tokens are the pieces of text a model counts, about three-quarters of a word).

What comes back is, for each question, one answer and a probability for it, from 0 to 1. Coding a text with three questions gives three rows. You can sort by the probability and read the uncertain rows first.

What a decision model cannot do is explain itself. It gives no reasons, no summaries and no free text, and every possible answer must be listed before you ask. For explanations, quotes or open labels you still need a chat model.

Several vendors have launched decision models in 2026. Jev, from TypeSafe, came out on 2026-09-15. Clef, from Cloudflare, followed on 2026-10-01 and can run on your own computer through Ollama. OpenAI's Decisions API entered beta on 2026-10-06 and became generally available on 2026-10-22. Google's Gemini Decision 1 launched on 2026-11-11.

**tidyllm** gives these models one interface, `decide()`: you write the questions once and change only the provider to switch between them.

We code eight synthetic survey answers with three questions at once (economy, topic and writer dissatisfaction), then compare results from Jev, OpenAI, and Gemini. We use the returned probabilities to identify answers for a second look; all figures come from live calls on 2026-11-13.

Every call that needs an API key is shown in a chunk that is not evaluated. Right after it, a second chunk loads the saved results of that call. A provider is the company whose server runs the model; an API key is your password for it; the [Get Started](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm.html) page lists where to get one. Rerunning requires `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `GOOGLE_API_KEY`.

## How far to trust a probability

A probability is *calibrated* when it matches how often the answer is right: of the answers given at 0.95, about 95 percent should be correct. Treat the number as a ranking first, and check its calibration on your own data.

In the [classifier article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_classifiers.html), 60 occupation answers were checked against human labels. Answers above 0.95 were right 92 to 100 percent of the time, and answers between 0.5 and 0.8 were right 60 to 69 percent of the time. Read the low rows first.

## When to use it instead of `chat()`

Use `decide()` when each text, image or recording needs an answer from a fixed set and you want a number to sort by. Use `chat()` when you need written text: an explanation, a summary, a quote, or a label you cannot list in advance.

`chat()` can also return answers in a fixed format, but without a probability and more slowly; the timings are further down. Use the table to match your task to the verb.

| What you need | Use |
|---|---|
| An explanation, a summary or a quote | `chat()` |
| A closed answer and a number to sort by, about a text, an image, a recording or a PDF | `decide()` |
| A free description of an image or a PDF | `chat()` |

## Write your questions as a schema

You tell the model what to answer by writing each question as one field of a schema, which is a named list of questions. The field description is the question text, and the field type fixes the kind of answer.

| Function | Question type | The answer is |
|---|---|---|
| `field_lgl()` | yes/no | `yes` or `no` |
| `field_fct(.levels = )` | choice | one of your levels |
| `field_fct(.levels = , .ordered = TRUE)` | score | one of your levels; the order of the levels is the scale |

Only these two helpers define questions. Other field types, and free text, return an error. The [Working with Structured Outputs section](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm.html) of Get Started explains schemas in general, and [the field helpers](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/reference/field_chr.html) list every argument.

Start with one yes/no question. Its description is the criterion: it says what counts as an answer about economic policy.

```{r q_economy}
questions <- tidyllm_schema(
  about_economy = field_lgl("Does the answer mainly concern economic policy such as wages, taxes, rents or pensions?")
)
```

For a yes/no question you can also say what yes and no mean, with `.true` and `.false`. Give both or neither.

```{r q_defined}
tidyllm_schema(
  about_economy = field_lgl("Does the answer mainly concern economic policy?",
    .true  = "Wages, taxes, rents, pensions or prices are the main subject",
    .false = "Another subject, or no policy subject at all")
)
```

A choice question lists its categories. The model must pick one of them, so add a `"none"` level for texts that fit no category.

```{r q_topic}
questions <- tidyllm_schema(
  about_economy = field_lgl("Does the answer mainly concern economic policy such as wages, taxes, rents or pensions?"),
  topic         = field_fct("Which topic does the answer mainly address?",
    .levels = c("housing", "labour", "taxes", "pensions", "migration", "climate", "none"))
)
```

A score question puts ordered levels on a scale, from lowest to highest. Here the scale runs from no dissatisfaction to strong dissatisfaction.

```{r q_score}
questions <- tidyllm_schema(
  about_economy   = field_lgl("Does the answer mainly concern economic policy such as wages, taxes, rents or pensions?"),
  topic           = field_fct("Which topic does the answer mainly address?",
    .levels = c("housing", "labour", "taxes", "pensions", "migration", "climate", "none")),
  dissatisfaction = field_fct("How strongly does the writer express dissatisfaction with current policy?",
    .levels = c("none", "mild", "strong"), .ordered = TRUE)
)
```

Models answer better when they know what each option means. `.level_descriptions` takes one short phrase per level. This is the schema the rest of the article uses.

```{r questions_full}
questions <- tidyllm_schema(
  about_economy   = field_lgl("Does the answer mainly concern economic policy such as wages, taxes, rents or pensions?"),
  topic           = field_fct("Which topic does the answer mainly address?",
    .levels = c("housing", "labour", "taxes", "pensions", "migration", "climate", "none"),
    .level_descriptions = c("Rents, house prices, housing supply", "Wages, jobs, working conditions",
      "Tax rates and who pays them", "Pensions and old-age provision",
      "Immigration and integration", "Climate and energy policy", "No policy topic named")),
  dissatisfaction = field_fct("How strongly does the writer express dissatisfaction with current policy?",
    .levels = c("none", "mild", "strong"), .ordered = TRUE,
    .level_descriptions = c("No complaint", "Some criticism, measured tone", "Anger or a demand for urgent change"))
)
```

For a score question, list the levels from lowest to highest. Very short texts need a framing line that says what the material is, such as "Survey question: What is your job? Answer: ...". The [classifier article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_classifiers.html) shows what happens without it.

## Ask one text

The eight synthetic survey answers are stored in `decide_answers.rds` beside this article. They cover rent, wages, pensions and other policy views.

```{r answers_load}
answers <- read_rds("decide_answers.rds")

answers
```

One call returns one row per question. The `type` column says whether the question was `yes_no`, `choice` or `score`. Run the first answer through Jev and look at the three rows.

```{r one_call, eval = FALSE}
one <- decide(answers$text[1], questions, jev())
```

```{r one_call_saved, echo = FALSE}
one <- read_rds("decide_one.rds")
one
```

The model says yes to the economy question at 0.96, names housing as the topic at 1.00, and reports strong dissatisfaction at 1.00. For a score question, `score` is the average level position, weighted by the probabilities and counted from zero. On three levels, 2 means strong.

A current call returns two more columns that the saved result above predates. `confidence` is the model's own confidence in the answer. `probabilities` holds the probability of every option, so you can see the runner-up: a 0.55 answer with a 0.40 runner-up is a closer call than one with five options at 0.20 each.

The tibble also carries three pieces of information that are not columns. R calls them attributes: `usage` (the tokens sent and returned), `latency` (the seconds the call took, from sending to reply) and `model` (the model that answered).

```{r one_attrs}
attributes(one)[c("usage", "latency", "model")]
```

This call used 503 input tokens and 107 output tokens, took 0.613 seconds and ran on `jev-1.14.0`. It was the first call of the run, so it was slower; later calls took about 0.2 seconds.

## Many texts at once

Pass a character vector and `decide()` codes every text. The calls run in parallel, five at a time by default, and come back as one tibble. A leading `state` column holds the text (cut to 60 characters) and `state_id` numbers the texts in the order you gave them.

```{r code_all, eval = FALSE}
many <- decide(answers$text, questions, jev())
```

```{r code_all_saved, echo = FALSE}
many <- read_rds("decide_many.rds")
```

A list works too. Every element of `.state` is one item, and an item is a string, an image, a message built with `llm_message()`, or a list of parts that belong together. A named list uses its names as the `state` labels. One call with a single item, however you pass it, returns the plain tibble from the previous section, without `state` and `state_id`.

Join the results to your data by `state_id`. The `coded` table then has one row per answer and question, with `id` linking it to the respondent.

```{r join_ids}
coded <- answers |>
  mutate(state_id = row_number()) |>
  left_join(many, by = "state_id")

coded |>
  select(id, question, answer, probability) |>
  slice_head(n = 6)
```

A text that fails, because the provider is down or refuses the request, gives one row of `NA` per question and one warning. The other texts keep their results, so rerun only the failed `state_id` values. If you meet rate-limit errors, lower `.max_active`; a free Gemini key allows about 200 requests a minute.

For regression you want one row per respondent. `pivot_wider()` puts each question in its own column; look for one row per answer, with `about_economy`, `topic` and `dissatisfaction` next to `id`.

```{r wide_table}
wide <- coded |>
  select(id, question, answer) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = question, values_from = answer)

wide
```

Join `wide` to the respondent data by `id`. The probabilities stay in `coded`, which the next sections use.

The long table also gives counts by question and answer.

```{r answer_counts}
coded |>
  count(question, answer)
```

Economy answers split evenly, with four yes and four no. Dissatisfaction has three none, two mild and three strong answers; topic has two none answers and one in each other category.

Speed is the reason to use a decision model for many texts. Coding the eight answers one call at a time with `decide(jev())` took 1.9 seconds; 40 answers took 8.0 and 8.7 seconds, about 0.2 seconds per text. The parallel call above took `r round(attr(many, "latency"), 2)` seconds for all eight. Eight `chat(openai())` calls one at a time took 18.9 and 21.7 seconds, or 2.4 to 2.7 seconds per text. All timings are from 2026-11-13 on one machine in Germany.

## Read the uncertain rows first

Four of the 24 answers have a probability below 0.8. That cut-off is a convenient round number, not a rule. Every other probability in this run is 0.85 or higher.

```{r low_prob}
coded |>
  filter(probability < 0.8) |>
  select(id, question, answer, probability) |>
  arrange(probability)
```

Two of these rows, ids 4 and 6, are where the three providers disagree later. Ids 5 and 7 are judgement calls on which they agree.

## Images, audio and PDFs

Many research materials are not text: photos in a survey, a recorded interview, a scanned letter. `decide()` reads them when the provider can, with the same questions and the same result tibble. Ask `provider_capabilities()` what each provider reads.

```{r media_capabilities}
provider_capabilities(.what = "decide_media") |>
  filter(supported) |>
  summarise(reads = paste(media, collapse = ", "), .by = provider)
```

Jev and OpenAI read images, and Gemini reads images, audio, video and PDFs. Ollama reads images through the same call; that route is new and has not run against a live server yet. A provider that cannot read a file type stops with a message before anything is sent. A PDF sent to a provider that does not read PDFs goes as its extracted text instead.

Wrap a file in `img()` to give `decide()` a picture. The question refers to "the picture" because the picture is the only thing the model sees.

```{r image_one, eval = FALSE}
cat_question <- tidyllm_schema(
  cat = field_lgl("Is the animal in the picture a cat?")
)

decide(img("photos/cat.jpg"), cat_question, openai(.detail = "low"))
```

Pictures cost more tokens than short texts. `.detail = "low"` tells OpenAI to read the picture at lower resolution; in our tests one photo cost about 1,500 input tokens by default and about 350 at low detail. Gemini has the same switch under the name `.resolution`.

To ask about several files together, put them into one item: a named list inside the outer `list()`. The names label the parts, so the questions can say "photo_a" and "photo_b".

```{r image_two, eval = FALSE}
pets <- tidyllm_schema(
  a_dog = field_lgl("Is the animal in photo_a a dog?"),
  b_dog = field_lgl("Is the animal in photo_b a dog?")
)

decide(list(list(photo_a = img("photos/cat.jpg"), photo_b = img("photos/dog.jpg"))), pets, jev())
```

An item can mix text and media, for example a caption followed by its photo: `list(list("Caption: found in the garden", img("photos/cat.jpg")))`. Before sending anything, `decide()` checks image size, format and count against the provider's limits and tells you which item is out of range. It never resizes an image for you.

To code many pictures, pass a list with one image per element; each element is its own item.

```{r image_many, eval = FALSE}
files <- list.files("photos", pattern = "jpg$", full.names = TRUE)

decide(map(files, img), cat_question, gemini(.resolution = "low"))
```

The `state` column then names each file, such as `[IMG] cat.jpg`. Pictures and recordings leave your computer and go to the provider, so do not send restricted or personal data, such as survey photos with faces.

## Choosing a provider

Each provider has a default model and a key you store in an environment variable. The price is the list price per million input tokens (the tokens you send).

| Provider call | Default model | Environment variable for your key | Reads | Price per million input tokens (USD) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `jev()` | `jev-latest` | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` | text, images | 0.042 |
| `openai()` | `gpt-6-luna` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | text, images | 0.10 |
| `gemini()` | `gemini-decision-1` | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | text, images, audio, video, PDFs | 0.10 |
| `ollama()` | `clef-flash` | none (runs on your computer) | text, images | free |

These are list prices on 2026-11-13 multiplied by the input tokens measured for the eight answers, not invoice figures. The calls used 499 input tokens with Jev, 481 with OpenAI and 292 with Gemini. Coding 10,000 survey answers costs about 0.21 USD with `jev()`, 0.29 USD with `gemini()` and 0.48 USD with `openai()`. Token counts differ because each provider counts the text and the questions in its own way.

Ollama is a free program that runs models on your own computer, so texts never leave it. The `clef-flash` model needs Ollama 0.35.0 or newer and about 11 to 12 GB of disk space. The [local models article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_local_models.html) covers the setup. The call has the same shape as the others:

```{r ollama_call, eval = FALSE}
decide(answers$text[1], questions, ollama(.model = "clef-flash"))
```

To compare the three hosted providers, we ran the same eight answers through each and kept the answer, the latency (seconds per call), the input and output tokens and the model name.

```{r providers_run, eval = FALSE}
providers <- list(
  jev    = jev(),
  openai = openai(.model = "gpt-6-luna"),
  gemini = gemini(.model = "gemini-decision-1")
)

decide_with <- function(text, id, provider, name) {
  r <- decide(text, questions, provider)
  r |> mutate(
    id = id, provider = name,
    latency = attr(r, "latency"),
    input_tokens = attr(r, "usage")$input_tokens,
    output_tokens = attr(r, "usage")$output_tokens,
    model = attr(r, "model")
  )
}

run_provider <- function(provider, name) {
  map2(answers$text, answers$id, \(t, i) decide_with(t, i, provider, name)) |>
    list_rbind()
}

providers_res <- imap(providers, run_provider) |> list_rbind()
```

```{r providers_run_saved, echo = FALSE}
providers_res <- read_rds("decide_providers.rds")
```

The summary gives the number of texts, the median latency, the mean input tokens per call and the model name for each provider.

```{r providers_summary}
providers_res |>
  group_by(provider) |>
  summarise(
    calls = n_distinct(id),
    median_latency = median(latency),
    input_tokens_per_call = mean(input_tokens),
    model = first(model)
  )
```

Median latency was 0.211 seconds for Jev, 0.215 seconds for Gemini and 0.231 seconds for OpenAI. The `model` is `NA` for Gemini because these results were recorded before `decide()` filled in `gemini-decision-1` when a reply names no model.

Next, keep only the answers on which the providers differ, with Jev's probability for each. Look at where the three columns split.

```{r providers_disagree}
jev_probability <- providers_res |>
  filter(provider == "jev") |>
  select(id, question, jev_probability = probability)

providers_res |>
  select(id, provider, question, answer) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = provider, values_from = answer) |>
  filter(!(jev == openai & openai == gemini)) |>
  left_join(jev_probability, by = c("id", "question"))
```

All three providers agree on 22 of the 24 answers. Agreement between models is not accuracy: the [classifier article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_classifiers.html) compares the answers with human labels.

The only disagreements are between neighbouring levels of the score question. For text 4, Jev says strong while OpenAI and Gemini say mild. For text 6, Jev and Gemini say strong while OpenAI says mild. Jev's probabilities for these answers were 0.74 and 0.62.

## When a call fails

Some problems stop `decide()` before anything is sent. The first call below passes an empty text; the second asks a choice question with a single level. The last line of each message says what to fix.

```{r errors, eval = FALSE}
decide("", questions, jev())

one_level <- tidyllm_schema(a = field_fct("pick", .levels = "only"))
decide(answers$text[1], one_level, jev())
```

The first message ends with `` strings must be non-empty ``. The second ends with `` Question `a` needs field_fct(.levels = ) with at least two levels. `` With many texts, the message also names the position, such as "State 3 of 8", so you can find the bad entry.

Other problems happen after sending: the provider is down, a request times out, or the model gives no answer to a question. Then `decide()` returns `NA` in `answer`, `probability` and `score` for what is missing, keeps everything else, and warns once.

A *dry run* builds the request and stops before sending it. It needs no API key and costs nothing, so you can check what would be sent. With many texts it returns a list with one request per text.

```{r dry_run}
request <- decide(answers$text[1], questions, jev(), .dry_run = TRUE)

request$url
```

## What `decide()` does not do

- **It does not check itself.** Label a random sample by hand and compare it with the model's answers. The [classifier article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_classifiers.html) shows this validation workflow.
- **It is not perfectly repeatable.** Jev probabilities shifted by 0.01 to 0.04 between our runs without changing any answer. OpenAI and Gemini repeated identically in the classifier article's test.
- **Not every provider reads every file type.** Check `provider_capabilities(.what = "decide_media")`, and expect a message instead of a result when the file type is not supported.
- **It sends your data away.** Texts, images and recordings go to the provider you choose. Use `ollama()` for material that must stay on your machine.

## What to take away

- **Use `decide()` for closed questions:** Choose it when each text, image or recording needs an answer from fixed options and you want a number to sort by.
- **Treat each field as a question:** Set the levels in scale order for a score question, and add descriptions so the model knows what each level means.
- **Pass many items at once:** A character vector or a list of items runs in parallel and returns one tibble with `state` and `state_id`.
- **Give it pictures when the question is about a picture:** Wrap files in `img()`, name the parts when a question must tell them apart, and check `provider_capabilities()` for what each provider reads.
- **Review uncertain answers first:** Read rows with low probabilities, then compare a human-labelled sample with the model's answers.
- **Choose and inspect your provider:** Compare measured price and speed, and use `.dry_run = TRUE` to inspect the request before sending it.

For a full workflow with codebooks, a second decision model, a stronger review pass and a human-labelled sample, see [Classifying Texts with tidyllm](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_classifiers.html); it checks `decide()` against human labels on 60 occupation answers.
